params.question: Which property of amyloid fibrils explains both their resistance to enzymatic breakdown and their ability to accumulate indefinitely in tissues?

answers.text: Their binding to serum amyloid P component

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SAP binds all amyloid universally and enables scintigraphic imaging, but it is not the structural basis for resistance to proteolysis. The cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation is what makes amyloid insoluble and resistant to enzymatic breakdown.

Correct. The cross-beta-pleated sheet — with beta strands stacking perpendicular to the fibril axis — creates a tightly packed scaffold that is insoluble in physiological salt solutions and resistant to enzymatic degradation, explaining why amyloid accumulates indefinitely once deposited.

Amyloid fibrils are highly ordered, not random. Their cross-beta-pleated sheet arrangement — with beta strands perpendicular to the fibril axis — is precisely what confers insolubility and resistance to enzymatic breakdown.

answers.text: Their eosinophilic appearance on haematoxylin and eosin staining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Eosinophilia on H&E is a histological observation, not the structural basis for durability. The cross-beta-pleated sheet conformation is the structural feature that makes amyloid fibrils resistant to degradation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Recall that amyloid's defining structural feature — the cross-beta-pleated sheet with beta strands perpendicular to the fibril axis — is what makes it insoluble and resistant to enzymatic breakdown.
The cross-beta-pleated sheet is the universal structural backbone of all amyloid — it explains both resistance to proteolysis and the characteristic Congo red apple-green birefringence.

params.question: A 60-year-old woman with suspected systemic amyloidosis needs tissue confirmation. Which biopsy approach should be attempted first?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Renal biopsy is an organ biopsy reserved for cases where less invasive sites are negative. The first-line approach is abdominal fat pad aspiration, offering approximately 80 per cent sensitivity with minimal morbidity.

Correct. Abdominal fat pad aspiration is the first-choice biopsy for suspected systemic amyloidosis — approximately 80 per cent sensitive and minimally invasive. Congo red staining of the aspirate, examined under polarised light for apple-green birefringence, confirms the diagnosis.

Bone marrow biopsy may follow when AL amyloidosis is suspected and less invasive sites are negative. Abdominal fat pad aspiration is the recommended initial step due to its high sensitivity (~80%) and minimal invasiveness.

Liver biopsy carries a risk of haemorrhage, particularly in amyloidotic livers which may be friable. Abdominal fat pad aspiration, with approximately 80 per cent sensitivity, is the preferred and less invasive first-line approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: For suspected systemic amyloidosis, follow the biopsy hierarchy: fat pad aspiration first (~80% sensitivity), then rectal submucosal biopsy, then organ biopsy if both are negative.
Abdominal fat pad aspiration is the first-choice biopsy — approximately 80 per cent sensitive, minimally invasive, and confirmed by Congo red staining under polarised light.

params.question: A patient has biopsy-confirmed amyloid in the kidneys, heart, and peripheral nerves. Serum protein electrophoresis shows no monoclonal protein, but the patient has had active rheumatoid arthritis for 15 years. Which analysis of these findings is most accurate?

answers.text: The absent monoclonal protein and long-standing chronic inflammation together make AA amyloidosis the most likely diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. A normal serum protein electrophoresis argues against AL amyloidosis, which typically produces a monoclonal M-spike. Fifteen years of active rheumatoid arthritis provides the sustained inflammatory stimulus that drives SAA overproduction, depositing as AA amyloid across multiple organs.

answers.text: Multi-organ involvement indicates AL amyloidosis regardless of the electrophoresis result

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Multi-organ deposition occurs in both AL and AA amyloidosis. The serum protein electrophoresis and clinical history are essential for distinguishing between them — here, the absent M-spike and chronic inflammation point to AA, not AL.

answers.text: The normal electrophoresis confirms this is localised amyloidosis despite multi-organ deposits

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Multi-organ deposition by definition indicates systemic, not localised, amyloidosis. Localised disease is confined to a single organ, such as amyloid-beta in the brain or calcitonin-derived amyloid in the thyroid.

answers.text: The peripheral neuropathy proves this is heredofamilial ATTR amyloidosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Although ATTR amyloidosis can cause neuropathy, a single finding should not override the full clinical picture. Renal involvement combined with 15 years of active rheumatoid arthritis and a normal SPEP fits AA amyloidosis far more convincingly.

overallFeedback.feedback: Analyse the findings systematically: no monoclonal protein on SPEP argues against AL, while 15 years of active rheumatoid arthritis is the classic driver of SAA overproduction in AA amyloidosis.

Systematic analysis — absent M-spike plus long-standing chronic inflammation — points to AA amyloidosis. The precursor SAA is driven by the rheumatoid arthritis, depositing as amyloid in kidneys, heart, and nerves.
